body: He gets in from work at ten past six on a Thursday and there are eleven people in the house. Nobody rang. His sister is there with her two, an aunt he has not seen since Easter is asleep in the good chair with her shoes off, and somebody has put the big pot on. The folding table that lives behind the freezer in the garage is up in the hall, carried in and opened without one word of discussion. He eats standing up, because a plate is in his hand before his coat is off. By nine the aunt has been driven home and a nephew is asleep across the arm of the sofa.

Nothing about that evening was arranged and nothing about it was unusual. It is a household operating as one body, in which presence needs no invitation, because the edge of the family is not drawn where the paperwork draws it.

Every media company on earth knows that Latino audiences are family-oriented, and every one of them reads that as a targeting instruction. Put more generations in the advert. Schedule around the hours families are together. It is not wrong. It is entirely external.

What it describes is behaviour, and what produces the behaviour is a doctrine. Underneath the full house and the folding table is a settled conviction about what a person actually is. The household, not the individual, is the unit that things happen to. Faith is inherited inside it rather than acquired outside it. Decisions are made in it rather than reported to it once they are final. Obligation runs sideways and upward as well as downward, so a cousin has claims on you and so does your mother-in-law, and neither is negotiable on the grounds that you are busy. Who counts as family is set by relationship, not by documentation. Call somebody your tía long enough and she is, and no registry records the change.

This band carries 121 stations across 29 languages, 40 of them international, one frequency to one language and no sharing. That structure was chosen for the same reason this article exists: a language is not a setting on a station, and neither is a household.

Programming for a household is more expensive than programming for a listener, and the expense is not in the music. It is in everything you have to give up. You cannot optimise for one ear, and you cannot let the schedule drift towards whichever segment is most valuable, because the room contains an eleven-year-old, her father and her grandmother at once and all three are the audience. You lose the ability to be edgy at nine in the evening and to be babyish at eight in the morning. You take the harder brief on purpose, because the household is the unit Scripture keeps addressing, and everywhere else has spent a century breaking it into individuals and selling to each.

That century of breaking has been so thorough that the pieces now look like the natural state of things. Every service in modern life is sold to one person and tuned to one person. Each member of a family has a separate account, a separate queue, a set of recommendations quietly diverging from everybody else in the building. The term for this is personalisation and it sounds like generosity. What it does is dissolve the last cheap way a household had of holding anything in common — that the same thing was audible in the same room to everybody at once. Nobody decided to end that. It was ended by small conveniences, each of them genuinely convenient.

The letters in the New Testament are not addressed the way our advertising is. They go to houses. Households are baptised, households are greeted by name, salvation comes to a house rather than to a resident of one, and a jailer is told a thing about himself and his household in a single breath as though the two were not separable. The whole apparatus of the private decision, reported to the family afterwards as news, would have taken a long time to explain to anybody in that text. It is not condemned there. It is simply not imagined.
So the question underneath the schedule is not who is listening. It is what a listener is.

The individual model deserves a fair hearing, because it exists for good reasons and it fixed real damage. Faith that is only ever inherited can become a family costume nobody inside it believes, held for the sake of the mother who would be wounded, and the conversion of a person who has never decided anything is a rumour rather than a fact. The insistence that each soul answers for itself broke the grip of some genuinely bad arrangements and rescued a great many people from their own relatives. All of that is true. What the individual model cannot do is transmit. It has no mechanism for handing a faith down a generation, because it defines the only real transaction as one that happens inside a single head. Then it is surprised, thirty years later, when nothing arrived.
A family is not an audience made of relatives.

He is thirty-four and he takes his mother to the hospital for the appointment about her eyes, because he took the day and his sister could not. He fills in the form on the clipboard, which asks him things in an order that makes no sense. At the desk the receptionist looks up and asks, kindly, whether he is the patient’s carer. He says he is her son. She says yes, but is he the registered carer. He stands there with the pen and finds that the honest answer needs a word the form does not contain — that nobody was appointed, that of course he is here because of course he is here — and says yes in the end, because the queue behind him is four people long.
There is no word on the form for what he is, because the form assumes a household is a group of individuals with service relationships between them. What he is, is part of a thing he did not join.

There is a real cost here and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. A household that operates like one body will absorb people who should have been let go, and will not let go of people who need to leave. It will keep somebody in a town they have outgrown. It will make an unwell relative everybody’s problem rather than anybody’s responsibility, and it will occasionally protect the wrong person out of a reflex that was designed to protect the vulnerable one.

Those failures are the failures of a thing that is load-bearing, which is not the same as the failure of a thing that is decorative. The individual model does not have those problems. It has the other set, and the other set is quieter and much larger: the relative nobody is obliged to collect, the old age spent alone with excellent personalised services, the faith that was never handed to anybody because handing was not part of the design. Every arrangement fails somewhere. It is worth choosing which failure you would rather have.

So a station built on this is not doing demographics with better manners. It is programming for the unit it believes is actually there — a room with several ages in it, several volumes of opinion, and one pot on the stove — instead of for one listener alone in a pair of headphones. That decision shows up in the music, in the hours it keeps, and in what it declines to play at eight in the evening when the whole house is passing through the kitchen.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

There are two Spanish frequencies on this dial and they are not duplicates. Jubilee Prayers in Spanish holds HM 350.50 — continuous oración and the Salmos, anchored in Madrid — and it is assigned and not yet on air, so there is nothing to hear there today. The other one has been broadcasting for some time, and it is the one this whole article has been describing.

Start at HM 320.30 — Familia Inspire (Español), hosted by Santiago Inspire, relayed from Mexico City, Los Angeles and Miami. Look at what its schedule is clocked to and the argument becomes visible: Mañana Familia at eight in the morning and Familia de Noche at eight at night, which are precisely the two hours when a household is in one room rather than dispersed across four. It is not aimed at the Spanish-speaking individual and it is not a Spanish edition of an English station. It is Praise, Worship and CCM curated for a family across Latin America, Spain and the diaspora, on the assumption that more than one generation is within earshot and that none of them should have to leave the room.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card — open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays. It is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else there. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are really reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer, and do not audition it privately first. Put HM 320.30 on at eight in the evening, in the room everybody walks through, at a volume that reaches the hall. Do not tell anybody what it is or ask what they think of it. If it belongs in your house you will find out the ordinary way — somebody will hum something in the car a fortnight later and not know where they got it, which is how a household has always learned anything worth keeping.
